prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep B042 as a single prize part for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case does not rest on all six of us ranking it first. It rests on a chain that is unusually complete and independently tested: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36) peptide, human incretin physiology, receptor biology, and then long-acting agonists with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. This is physiology in the sense the prize was designed for, and it is mature. No member disputes maturity. The citation I propose is deliberately about the physiology and the active form, not about a drug class, so it credits the discovery on which the therapeutics depend without asserting anything about who engineered which analogue.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and round 1 did not remove it. Knudsen is excluded by the three-name cap and her work on acylated, long-acting analogues was not routine. Habener's group is outside the credited names, and the Mojsov and Habener priority question cannot be settled from the shortlist. Every member who addressed it, including me, is working from recollection. A citation naming Mojsov asserts a contribution to the identification of the active form that the committee should be able to defend in writing. The prize could also be read as honouring a drug class, which the wording tries to avoid. I do not think any of this outweighs the science, but I would not call the trio the only fair set.

responses.point: Perlmann warned that three of us writing the same trio must not turn a shared recollection of the Mojsov and Habener history into a settled fact, and asked whether a committee with proper sources would still find Mojsov's contribution to the active form distinguishable from the proglucagon work.
responses.response: This is the right correction to my round-1 statement, where I called the active-peptide priority a recollection but still wrote it as if it were secure. My own recollection is that the proglucagon sequence and cloning work belongs largely to the Habener group, while Mojsov's distinct claim is the identification and synthesis of the shorter, biologically active GLP-1(7-36) form. That separates the two claims, and the citation wording I propose follows it. I cannot verify it here. So I treat it as a condition: I keep Mojsov because the discovery is the active form and not the gene, but if the committee had a record showing that the active-form identification was not distinguishable from the proglucagon work, I would move Knudsen into the third place and reword.

responses.point: Linnarsson, having moved to the Drucker, Holst and Mojsov trio, says that drug engineering is not lesser in principle, that Knudsen's omission is a real cost, and that he accepts the trio because it is the most coherent set around one discovery narrative and not because it is the only fair one.
responses.response: I agree, and I withdraw any suggestion in my round-1 answer that the setting of the work, industrial or academic, bears on weight. In round 1 I said Knudsen's work was development, and that undersold it. Extending the half-life of a peptide degraded within minutes was the step that made the biology usable. My reason for not naming her is only the cap and the discovery criterion. I would put that on record in the same terms you use. On the chair's question about the third name, my answer is conditional: Mojsov if the active-form claim holds, and Knudsen if it does not. I would not take the middle path of a two-name prize, because Holst and Drucker alone omit the identification of the active peptide, which is the step that gave the drug designers a defined target.

responses.point: The chair asked whether the B042 citation should name only the physiology and the active peptide or also acknowledge long-acting agonists, and favoured wording that avoids asserting a priority the committee cannot adjudicate.
responses.response: I support keeping the citation on the physiology and the active form and have changed my wording to match yours: 'physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form'. 'Active forms' in my round-1 text implied more than I can support. The therapy appears only as the consequence ('which made possible incretin-based treatment'), so the long-acting agonists are acknowledged without crediting engineering to the named laureates. If the committee wants the Knudsen arm acknowledged in the public text, I would do it in the accompanying background and not by changing the credited names. I would defend a single-part B042 prize, since no second part has a narrower attribution gap than the one in B042.

responses.point: El-Manira asked that the tool-versus-discovery question be answered once and applied consistently to B004 and B029, and argued that optogenetics rests on a discovery about a light-gated channel.
responses.response: The consistency request is fair, and I accept that I leaned on the word 'tool' too easily in round 1. My rule is this. A method qualifies if it rests on a discovery of a biological principle and has produced new knowledge across fields. A method that is mainly an engineering advance in measuring or reading out something already known qualifies less readily. By that rule B029 is better placed than B004, because channelrhodopsin function is a biological finding. It still does not outrank B042 for me, because of the six-name attribution problem and the early clinical translation. I therefore keep it as an alternative, in the form of Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, and I regard the omission of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck as a cost I cannot remove.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argued that the credit gaps in B038 (Eshhar, Kuwana) and B013 (Zhou) are comparable to B042's and should not push B042 down, and that pairing GLP-1 with CAR-T or anti-TNF would force the GLP-1 credit below three names.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The attribution gap in B042 is the narrowest of the shortlist, because the disputed credit concerns one name, and the alternatives have comparable or wider gaps. Her second point is the decisive practical argument against a two-part prize. Giving the second part to B038 or B041 would require cutting the GLP-1 credit to two people, and each of the three names covers a different step of the chain. I also note that she did not answer my round-1 question on B041, namely what the single Nobel-level discovery is beyond clinical proof. I keep it outside my alternatives. My view of it as mature and overdue is unchanged.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1(7-36) form is clearly distinguishable from the proglucagon work of the Habener group. I rely on recollection and no member has checked a primary source.
Whether the committee wants the physiology alone credited, in which case Mojsov is the third name, or the drug-development step, in which case Knudsen is. My answer depends on the first uncertainty.
Whether B038 carries a cleaner claim than B029 as the second alternative once Eshhar's omission and the separation of Rosenberg's work from CAR engineering are weighed.
Whether the tool-versus-discovery rule I stated is applied the same way to B004 and B029 by the rest of the committee.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisen and share Karolinska Institutet with several members. None of the shortlisted discoveries involves my own work or a collaborator of mine, and I do not treat shared affiliation as a conflict. Linnarsson's methodological reliance on sequencing (B004) is not a tie to me, and B004 is not part of my configuration.
